THOUGHT: This 5-day-old exclusively breastfed male newborn presents with progressive jaundice starting on the face and spreading to the trunk, accompanied by scleral icterus — classic clinical signs of hyperbilirubinemia. Total serum bilirubin is 7 mg/dL, which is elevated for a 5-day-old (though not yet in the high-risk range per AAP guidelines; 95th percentile at 120 hours ≈ 12–13 mg/dL). However, the pattern, timing, and feeding history are key. Jaundice appearing after 24 hours of life and peaking between days 3–5 is typical of unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinemia. The direct (conjugated) bilirubin is only 0.6 mg/dL (i.e., ~8.5% of total), confirming predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia — consistent with physiologic or breastfeeding-related jaundice, not hepatobiliary disease or conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (e.g., biliary atresia, metabolic disorders). Reticulocyte count is low (0.3%), making hemolysis unlikely (would expect >2–3% in significant hemolysis). Hemoglobin is normal (17.6 g/dL), further arguing against acute hemolysis. Maternal blood group is A, Rh-negative; fetal is O, Rh-positive — this combination carries risk for anti-Rh (anti-D) hemolytic disease, but the infant is Rh-positive and mother Rh-negative *without mention of prior sensitization or prophylaxis* — however, the reticulocyte count and absence of anemia make significant Rh isoimmunization improbable. Also, ABO incompatibility (mother A, baby O) is not possible — baby is type O, mother is type A; ABO hemolysis typically occurs when mother is O and baby is A or B (maternal anti-A/B IgG crosses placenta). So ABO incompatibility is unlikely here. Free T4 is normal (7 μg/dL; normal neonatal range ~6–13 μg/dL), making congenital hypothyroidism an unlikely contributor. The exclusive breastfeeding every 2–3 hours suggests adequate intake, but even with good feeding, some infants develop “breastfeeding jaundice” (due to relative caloric insufficiency or delayed stooling leading to enterohepatic circulation) or “breast milk jaundice” (peaks later, ~day 5–7, due to β-glucuronidase in breast milk or other factors). Given the onset on day 4–5, progression, otherwise well appearance, normal vital signs, and lab findings (mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, no anemia, low reticulocytes), the most likely diagnosis is breastfeeding-associated jaundice — a benign, common cause of indirect hyperbilirubinemia in the first week.

DIAGNOSIS: Breastfeeding-associated jaundice
